result:
I’ll write about one of the most ordinary and mysterious things in life: waiting.

Waiting is such a small word for such a large experience. We wait for trains, for emails, for test results, for people who said they were “five minutes away” half an hour ago. We wait for weather to change, for a mood to pass, for the right sentence to arrive, for grief to loosen its grip, for our own courage to become available. A life is, in many ways, a long sequence of waits, interrupted by moments of motion that often feel shorter than the waits themselves.

There is something unfair about waiting. It can make a person feel passive, as if they have been placed on a shelf and forgotten. Yet waiting is also where life does some of its deepest work. Seeds wait underground before they become visible. Bread waits in the oven, rising in silence. Musicians wait between notes, and that silence is part of the music. We tend to think of action as the only place where meaning lives, but waiting is often where meaning ripens.

I think people dislike waiting because it puts them face to face with time. When we are busy, time becomes a tool, something we use to get from one thing to another. But in waiting, time becomes an environment. It surrounds us. We cannot easily ignore it. We begin to notice its texture: slow minutes, elastic hours, the strange way some days seem to contain too much and others too little. Waiting forces an encounter with our own impatience, and impatience is one of the most honest emotions we have. It tells us that we want something now, not later, and that the gap between now and later feels uncomfortably real.

Children are better at waiting than adults in one important way: they do not disguise their frustration. They fidget, complain, ask the same question repeatedly, and refuse to pretend that patience is effortless. Adults, by contrast, often wrap waiting in language that sounds noble. We say we are “being patient,” “keeping perspective,” “letting things unfold,” which is sometimes true, but sometimes simply a polished name for wanting something very much and not having it yet. Still, there is dignity in both versions. The child’s open impatience is a form of honesty. The adult’s practiced endurance is a form of discipline. Both are human.

Waiting can be lonely. There are waits you share with others—standing in line, sitting in a hospital corridor, refreshing the same page on a phone while friends do the same—and these shared waits can create a peculiar fellowship. Strangers look at one another and know, without speaking, that everyone in the room has been recruited into the same temporary uncertainty. But there are also private waits that no one sees: waiting for someone to love you back, waiting for a career to begin, waiting for your body to feel like yours again, waiting for an apology that may never come. Those waits are heavy because they are invisible. You can carry them in a crowd and appear untouched.

What makes waiting difficult is not only the passage of time but the imagination. When we wait, we begin to construct possible futures. Some are hopeful, some catastrophic, most are absurdly detailed. The mind becomes a small theater of previews, rehearsing joy, disappointment, relief, embarrassment, and every possible variation in between. In this way, waiting can be more exhausting than the event itself. The appointment lasts fifteen minutes; the anticipation lasts three days. The phone call lasts two minutes; the dread leading up to it lasts all afternoon. Our imaginations are gifted, but they are not always kind.

And yet waiting can become a kind of sanctuary. There are forms of waiting that are restful, even sacred. Think of sitting by a window in the late afternoon, not needing to do anything, watching light change the color of a wall. Think of waiting beside someone you love in a quiet room, neither of you speaking, both of you simply sharing the fact of being there. Think of the pause before a performance begins, when the hall is full of expectant silence. In those moments, waiting is not a lack but a presence. It is the held breath before a song.

Some people spend years waiting for their lives to begin, as if real life is always elsewhere, just around the corner, one promotion away, one relationship away, one breakthrough away. That belief can be cruel. It turns the present into a corridor rather than a room. You keep moving through it without ever unpacking. But life is not waiting for you to catch up; it is happening even in the delays, even in the setbacks, even in the ordinary Tuesday that seems to offer nothing dramatic at all. The challenge is not to eliminate waiting—that is impossible—but to inhabit it without surrendering your whole attention to the future.

This is easier said than done. I don’t know a single person who has mastered waiting. Some people distract themselves. Some become furious. Some develop rituals: pacing, checking, counting, making lists, cleaning a kitchen drawer, rearranging books, reading the same paragraph over and over. These are not merely habits; they are negotiations with uncertainty. Humans are excellent at inventing little bridges over the river of not knowing.

Perhaps that is the deepest truth about waiting: it is a relationship with not knowing. We are so often tempted to believe that certainty would solve our problems, but certainty has its own cost. It would flatten the world into something predictable, and predictability, while comforting, can be dull. Uncertainty keeps us awake. It keeps us humble. It reminds us that we do not control everything and never have. This is frightening, but it is also the condition under which surprise becomes possible.

Waiting, then, is a strange teacher. It teaches humility because it reminds us that our will is not the whole story. It teaches attention because if we cannot hurry time, we may as well notice what is in front of us. It teaches endurance, which is not the same as cheerfulness, and not the same as resignation. Endurance is the art of remaining present while the world refuses to proceed on our preferred schedule.

One day, of course, the waiting ends. The train arrives. The message comes. The doctor speaks. The interview is over. The storm passes. The person returns or does not return. We move from anticipation into fact, from possibility into reality, and for a moment the mind goes quiet, almost startled by the arrival of what it had been preparing for. But even then, another wait begins, because life does not provide a final stillness. It only gives us temporary answers.

Maybe that is why waiting feels so human. It is a rehearsal for the larger mystery of being alive: that we are always in the middle of something, always between before and after, always learning how to live without full access to the ending. And maybe that is enough.
